title: Accounting Standard 26 Intangible Assets
outcomes: Identify intangible assets and their recognition criteria.
Distinguish research from development and apply capitalisation criteria.
Identify costs that are always expensed.
Amortise intangibles and apply the ten-year presumption and impairment rules.

meta.exam_tip: Draw a phase timeline: research → development before criteria → development after criteria → available for use.

concepts.title: What an intangible asset is
body: An intangible asset is an identifiable, non-monetary asset with no physical form, that the enterprise uses to make goods or deliver services, to let out, or to run its administration.

Three features: identifiability (separable from goodwill), control (power to obtain benefits and restrict others' access, usually by legal rights), and future economic benefits (revenue or cost savings).

Examples: software, patents, copyrights, licences, franchises, import quotas, customer or supplier relationships, marketing rights. AS 26 does not cover financial assets, mineral rights, insurance contracts, goodwill on amalgamation (AS 14) and intangibles covered by other standards.
concepts.analogy: An asset you cannot touch but can identify, control and profit from.
concepts.work: Staff skills are not an intangible asset — the company cannot control them.

concepts.title: Recognition and initial measurement
body: An intangible is recognised only if it is probable that its expected economic benefits will flow to the enterprise and its cost can be measured reliably; it is then measured at cost.
Separately acquired: purchase price, import duties and non-refundable taxes, and directly attributable costs of preparing it for use.

Acquired in an amalgamation in the nature of purchase: at fair value if it can be measured reliably; otherwise it is included in goodwill. Acquired by exchange: fair value of what is given up; by government grant: under AS 12.
Later expenditure is added to cost only if it is likely to enable the asset to generate benefits beyond its originally assessed standard and can be measured reliably; otherwise it is expensed.
concepts.analogy: Recognise only what you can measure and expect to benefit from.
concepts.work: A licence bought for ₹10 lakh plus ₹50,000 legal fees is recorded at ₹10.5 lakh.

concepts.title: Internally generated intangibles: research and development
body: Internally generated goodwill is never recognised. Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and similar items are not recognised either, as their cost cannot be separated from building the business as a whole.
Research (original investigation to gain new knowledge) is always expensed.

Development (applying research to plan or design new or improved products or processes before commercial use) is capitalised only when all of these can be shown: technical feasibility of completion; intention to complete and use or sell; ability to use or sell; how it will generate probable benefits (a market or internal usefulness); adequate technical, financial and other resources; and ability to measure the expenditure reliably.

If research and development phases cannot be distinguished, all expenditure is treated as research. Cost of an internally generated intangible includes only expenditure from the date the criteria are first met; earlier expenses are not reinstated.
concepts.analogy: Think of research as exploring and development as building — only proven building is capitalised.
concepts.work: Designing a prototype that has passed technical tests may be development; searching for new materials is research.

concepts.title: Items always expensed
body: Expensed when incurred, even if they may bring future benefits: start-up costs (unless part of PPE cost), training, advertising and promotion, relocation or reorganisation, and expenditure on research.
Expenditure on an intangible item initially recognised as an expense is not later recognised as part of an asset's cost.
concepts.analogy: Some spending builds the business but cannot be capitalised.
concepts.work: A launch advertising campaign of ₹2 crore is an expense, however successful.

concepts.title: Amortisation, impairment and retirement
body: The depreciable amount is allocated systematically over the best estimate of useful life. There is a rebuttable presumption that the useful life does not exceed ten years from when the asset is available for use.

Amortisation starts when the asset is available for use. The method reflects the pattern of benefits consumed; if that cannot be determined reliably, straight-line is used. Residual value is assumed to be zero unless there is a commitment by a third party to buy it or an active market.

Amortisation period and method are revisited every year end. Where the life chosen is longer than ten years, recoverable amount is estimated at least annually, even without signs of impairment; AS 28 applies generally.
On retirement or disposal, the asset is derecognised and the gain or loss (net proceeds less carrying amount) goes to profit and loss.
concepts.analogy: Ten years is the default ceiling; going beyond it needs evidence and annual testing.
concepts.work: Software expected to be used for 4 years is amortised over 4, even if the licence is perpetual.

illustrations.title: From research to a product
illustrations.q: Medha Pharma Ltd. (year ends 31 March 2027) spent ₹12 lakh on research in April–June 2026 and ₹18 lakh on development in July–September 2026. All recognition criteria for development were first met on 1 October 2026; it then spent ₹30 lakh to December. The product was available for use on 1 January 2027 with a useful life of 5 years. Show the treatment.

checks.label: Expensed: research + development before criteria met (₹ lakh)

illustrations.title: Life of a purchased patent
illustrations.q: Arun Tech Ltd. bought a patent for ₹60,00,000. Its legal life is 12 years, but the technology is expected to be useful for only 8 years. Compute annual amortisation and say whether an annual recoverable amount test is needed.

head: Item
Working
Answer
rows: Shorter of legal life (12) and expected use (8)
solution.title: Amortisation

solution.text: The life is within the 10-year presumption, so the yearly recoverable amount test that applies to lives beyond 10 years is not required; normal AS 28 impairment indicators still apply.

jobs.title: R&D capitalisation review
jobs.situation: A tech client capitalised all R&D for a new app, including early user surveys and brand launch costs.
steps: Find the date all six criteria were met.
Remove launch, training and branding costs.
jobs.takeaway: The date the criteria are met is the gateway for capitalisation.

mcqs.q: Which can be recognised as an intangible asset?
options: A patent purchased from another company
mcqs.explain: A purchased patent is identifiable, controlled through legal rights and has a reliable cost. Internally generated goodwill and brands are not recognised, and staff skills are not controlled. In practice: check control first.

mcqs.q: Expenditure in the research phase is:
mcqs.explain: Research cannot show that an asset exists that will generate probable future benefits, so AS 26 requires all research expenditure to be expensed when incurred. In practice: keep phase-wise cost records.
mcqs.topic: Internally generated intangibles: research and development

mcqs.q: Development cost is capitalised only when the enterprise can demonstrate, among others:
options: Technical feasibility and ability to measure the expenditure reliably
That the product will sell at a profit in year one
mcqs.explain: All criteria must be met: technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use or sell, probable benefits, adequate resources and reliable measurement. Board approval alone is not enough. In practice: document each criterion.
mcqs.topic: Internally generated intangibles: research and development

mcqs.q: Development costs expensed before the criteria were met:
options: Cannot be reinstated as an asset later
Are reinstated when the criteria are met
mcqs.explain: Expenditure on an intangible item that was recognised as an expense in earlier periods stays an expense; it is never moved back into an asset's cost later. Capitalisation runs only from the date criteria are met. In practice: get the date right.
mcqs.topic: Internally generated intangibles: research and development

options: Cost of a purchased software licence
Directly attributable cost of preparing a patent for use
Development cost after criteria are met
mcqs.explain: AS 26 lists start-up, training, advertising and promotion, relocation and reorganisation costs as expenses when incurred, because they cannot be separated from developing the business as a whole. In practice: do not defer launch costs.

mcqs.q: The rebuttable presumption for the maximum useful life of an intangible asset is:
options: Ten years from when it is available for use
mcqs.explain: AS 26 assumes a useful life of at most ten years, counted from when the asset can first be used, unless persuasive evidence supports a longer life, in which case recoverable amount is tested annually. In practice: justify longer lives.

mcqs.q: Residual value of an intangible asset is normally assumed to be:
mcqs.explain: Residual value is taken as zero unless a third party has committed to buy the asset at the end of its life or there is an active market for it. In practice: most intangibles are amortised fully.

mcqs.q: A licence costing ₹40 lakh with a useful life of 5 years, available for use on 1 October (year ends 31 March). Amortisation for the first year:
mcqs.explain: Annual amortisation is ₹40 lakh ÷ 5 = ₹8 lakh; it starts when the asset is available for use, so six months gives ₹4 lakh. In practice: use straight-line if the pattern is unclear.

mcqs.q: If the useful life of an intangible asset is estimated beyond ten years, the enterprise must:
options: Estimate its recoverable amount at least annually
mcqs.explain: Where the presumption of ten years is rebutted, AS 26 requires the recoverable amount to be estimated at least at each financial year end, even with no indication of impairment, and the reasons disclosed. In practice: keep strong evidence.

mcqs.q: An intangible acquired in an amalgamation in the nature of purchase whose fair value cannot be measured reliably is:
options: Recognised at the transferor's book value
mcqs.explain: Such an intangible is recognised at fair value only when that can be measured reliably; otherwise it is not recognised separately and is subsumed in goodwill. In practice: get a valuation where possible.

questions.q: Medha Pharma Ltd. (year ends 31 March 2027) spent ₹12 lakh on research in April–June 2026 and ₹18 lakh on development in July–September 2026. All recognition criteria for development were first met on 1 October 2026; it then spent ₹30 lakh to December. The product was available for use on 1 January 2027 with a useful life of 5 years. Show the treatment.

checks.label: Expensed: research + development before criteria met (₹ lakh)

questions.q: Arun Tech Ltd. bought a patent for ₹60,00,000. Its legal life is 12 years, but the technology is expected to be useful for only 8 years. Compute annual amortisation and say whether an annual recoverable amount test is needed.

head: Item
Working
Answer
rows: Shorter of legal life (12) and expected use (8)
model.title: Amortisation

model.text: The life is within the 10-year presumption, so the yearly recoverable amount test that applies to lives beyond 10 years is not required; normal AS 28 impairment indicators still apply.

remarks: Economic life can be shorter than legal life.

summary: Identifiable, controlled, future benefits, no physical form.
Recognise if benefits probable and cost reliable; at cost.
No internally generated goodwill, brands, titles, customer lists.
Research expensed; development capitalised once all six criteria met.
Amortise from available for use; presumed life ≤ 10 years; annual test if longer.
traps: Legal life is not automatically useful life.

viva.model: It can be separated from the enterprise and its goodwill — sold, licensed or rented — or arises from contractual or legal rights.

viva.q: Why is internally generated goodwill not recognised?
viva.model: Because it is neither separable nor tied to legal rights, so it fails identifiability, and what it cost to build cannot be measured reliably.

viva.q: List the conditions for capitalising development cost.
viva.model: Technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use or sell, probable future benefits, adequate resources, and reliable measurement of expenditure.
From the date the intangible asset is available for use.

viva.q: Name two costs that are always expensed.
viva.model: Advertising and promotion, staff training, start-up costs, relocation and research expenditure.

cases.title: Navya Foods Ltd.
cases.case: Navya Foods Ltd. spent ₹50 lakh on TV ads for its new snack brand, ₹15 lakh on training its sales team and ₹40 lakh to buy the "Crunchy" brand from another company (expected useful life 6 years). It values its own brand "Navya" at ₹2 crore based on an expert report.

mcqs.q: The "Navya" brand valued by the expert is:
options: Not recognised, as it is internally generated
mcqs.explain: Internally generated brands are not recognised as intangible assets, as their cost cannot be distinguished from developing the business. An expert valuation does not change this. In practice: no entry is passed.
mcqs.topic: Internally generated intangibles: research and development

mcqs.q: Amount expensed this year from the ads and training:
mcqs.explain: Advertising (₹50 lakh) and training (₹15 lakh) are expensed as incurred under AS 26, giving ₹65 lakh. They cannot be capitalised even if they build the brand. In practice: show under other expenses.

mcqs.q: Annual amortisation of the purchased "Crunchy" brand:
mcqs.explain: A purchased brand is recognised at cost ₹40 lakh and amortised over its useful life of 6 years: ₹6.67 lakh a year, within the ten-year presumption. In practice: review the life yearly.
